sources.title: NHGRI: The cost of sequencing a human genome

grounding:
## Technology
- **emTech:** gene-sequencing
- **Product category:** Portable / clinic-rugged same-shift pathogen sequencers

## Capabilities
Same-shift or next-morning provisional pathogen reads when workflow, power, reagents, and trained staff exist — not sequencing as a capital-lab monopoly only.

## Trends & predictions
Time-to-read and ruggedness improve; reagent kits get cheaper; software turns raw reads into provisional signals for non-specialist posts. **Forecast (not lock):** same-shift reads become more routine at border and rural clinics through the late 2020s where power and training hold.

## Milestone
Cheaper, more field-rugged sequencers and software (through ~2026) make on-site clinic reads realistic for small posts.

## Honest limits
Power and cold chain after dusk; no full bioinformatics team; public trust fragile — pilot language only for 2026.
## Unlocks Use Case(s)
Local sample-to-read workflows; triage and isolation decisions without waiting on a distant lab truck.

## Applications
Clinic sample-to-isolation protocols; shift-handoff pathogen boards; trust-preserving result counseling workflows — invent the local system.

trends.name: Cost per human genome
trends.summary: It used to cost tens of thousands of dollars to read one person’s full DNA. After public labs were no longer the only buyers, that price has been dropping by about half every 18 months. The chart is US dollars per genome — lower means cheaper.

local.label: Outbreak
local.description: The fever pattern on the fridge sheet is real and still invisible while the swabs ride the weekly lab truck. Every day without an answer, the bench and the ward trade places.

support.label: Fear
support.description: Traders and travelers hear rumors before results. When the market empties on a guess, the clinic loses the trust it needs to isolate anyone.

mission.scene: Nurse Amina seals another swab and slides it into the cooler. The fever does not match the sheet on the fridge. The lab truck left at dawn. Answers take days. By then the queue has moved on — or the ward is full. Who can tell her what the fever is before the next queue arrives?
mission.briefMd:
## The place

Nurse Amina seals another swab under the corrugated awning at **Crossing Clinic 7**. Three nurses. A doctor on alternate days. A generator that coughs after midnight. Travelers and traders share one waiting bench.

She checks the fever sheet taped to the fridge. The pattern does not match. Last week it was children from the river side. This week it is drivers who slept in their cabs, and two of them are back for the second time.

Labeled tubes stack in the cooler. The weekly lab truck already rolled out at dawn. Central results return in days, not hours. By then the person on the bench has moved on. Or the ward is full. Rumors fill the gap first.

Dr. Okonkwo, who runs the clinic, has one call to make before the market opens. Close the bench and lose the traders' trust, or keep it open and guess. Neither choice is a diagnosis.

## The bigger problem

This is how outbreaks stay invisible. Truth lives in a capital lab. The calendar is a truck, not a shift. A clinic that sees the first cases is the last to know what they are.

While samples travel, rumors move first. The wrong ward fills. A market empties on a guess. The next traveler is already across the border. The root is not that this bench lacks a machine. It is a system that only believes a result after it has left the people who needed it, and gives them nothing to say in the meantime.

## Your job

Invent a way this clinic can know what the fever is before the next queue arrives. Stakeholder: **Dr. Okonkwo, clinic lead**.
